section.title: Crossing the Jordan
section.sectionRationale: The promise moves from word to wonder. Israel breaks camp and comes to the flooded Jordan, and God tells them exactly how they will cross: the priests carrying the ark of the covenant will step into the water, and the river will pile up so the whole nation can pass on dry ground. It is one movement, the miraculous crossing that mirrors the Red Sea, exalts Joshua before the people, and proves that the living God is among them.
section.thesis: As at the Red Sea, God parts the waters so His people may pass, but this time the ark of the covenant leads the way into the flood, teaching Israel that they enter the land only behind the presence of the living God, who goes ahead of them to drive out their enemies.
section.frameNote: Three beats: the command to follow the ark and consecrate themselves, verses 1 to 6; God's word exalting Joshua and promising the miracle, verses 7 to 13; and the priests stepping into the flood as the waters heap up and Israel crosses on dry ground, verses 14 to 17.

units.label: Follow the ark and consecrate yourselves
units.note: tomorrow the LORD will do wonders among you

verses.text: Early the next morning Joshua got up and left Shittim with all the Israelites. They went as far as the Jordan, where they camped before crossing over.
After three days the officers went through the camp
and commanded the people: “When you see the ark of the covenant of the LORD your God being carried by the Levitical priests, you are to set out from your positions and follow it.
But keep a distance of about two thousand cubits between yourselves and the ark. Do not go near it, so that you can see the way to go, since you have never traveled this way before.”
Then Joshua told the people, “{{qadash|Consecrate}} yourselves, for tomorrow the LORD will do wonders among you.”
And he said to the priests, “Take the {{aron|ark}} of the covenant and go on ahead of the people.” So they carried the ark of the covenant and went ahead of them.

units.label: God's word exalts Joshua and promises the miracle
units.note: this is how you will know that the living God is among you

verses.text: Now the LORD said to Joshua, “Today I will begin to exalt you in the sight of all Israel, so they may know that I am with you just as I was with Moses.
Command the priests carrying the ark of the covenant: ‘When you reach the edge of the waters, stand in the Jordan.’”
So Joshua told the Israelites, “Come here and listen to the words of the LORD your God.”

He continued, “This is how you will know that the {{chay|living}} God is among you and that He will surely drive out before you the Canaanites, Hittites, Hivites, Perizzites, Girgashites, Amorites, and Jebusites.
Behold, the ark of the covenant of the Lord of all the earth will go ahead of you into the Jordan.
Now choose twelve men from the tribes of Israel, one from each tribe.
When the feet of the priests who carry the ark of the LORD, the Lord of all the earth, touch down in the waters of the Jordan, its flowing waters will be cut off and will stand up in a heap.”

units.label: The priests step in and Israel crosses on dry ground
units.note: the priests stood firm on dry ground in the middle of the Jordan

verses.text: So when the people broke camp to cross the Jordan, the priests carried the ark of the covenant ahead of them.
Now the Jordan overflows its banks throughout the harvest season. But as soon as the priests carrying the ark reached the Jordan and their feet touched the water’s edge,

the flowing water stood still. It backed up as far upstream as Adam, a city in the area of Zarethan, while the water flowing toward the Sea of the Arabah (the Salt Sea) was completely cut off. So the people crossed over opposite Jericho.

The priests carrying the ark of the covenant of the LORD stood firm on dry ground in the middle of the Jordan, while all Israel crossed over the dry ground, until the entire nation had crossed the Jordan.

qadash.gloss: To consecrate, set apart, make holy. Before God acts, Joshua calls the people to consecrate themselves, to prepare to meet the holy God who is about to do wonders among them. The same call was given at Sinai, Exodus 19:10-15; encountering God's mighty presence always requires that His people be set apart and ready.

aron.gloss: The ark, the sacred chest overlaid with gold that held the tablets of the covenant and was crowned by the mercy seat. As the throne and sign of God's presence among Israel, the aron goes first into the Jordan; the people follow the presence of God into the land. It is the visible pledge that the LORD Himself leads the way.

chay.gloss: Living, alive. Israel will know that the living God is among them, in pointed contrast to the lifeless idols of Canaan. The God who cuts off a flooding river is not a carved image but the living Lord of all the earth, active and present, who will drive out the nations before His people.

basic.context: Israel leaves camp and reaches the Jordan, which is at flood stage during harvest season, a real barrier between them and the land. God gives clear instructions: the priests will carry the ark of the covenant, the sign of God's presence, and step into the river ahead of everyone. When their feet touch the water, the river will stop flowing and pile up, so the whole nation can walk across on dry ground. This is a deliberate echo of the Red Sea crossing under Moses, and God says it will prove two things: that He is with Joshua as He was with Moses, and that the living God is truly among His people. The question the passage answers is: how do God's people enter into what He has promised?
basic.hermeneutics: This is historical narrative recording a real miracle at a real river. It is not a template for expecting God to part rivers for us, but it teaches enduring truths: God leads His people by His presence, He requires them to be consecrated, and He confirms His chosen leaders. The crossing also functions symbolically in Scripture as a passage from the wilderness into the inheritance, a picture later writers draw on.
basic.originalLanguages: Joshua calls the people to qadash, to consecrate themselves, before God works. The aron, the ark, the throne of God's presence, goes first into the flood. And the whole event proves that the chay, the living God, is among them, unlike the dead idols of Canaan.
basic.typology: The ark leading Israel through the waters into the land pictures Christ, God's presence in the flesh, going before His people through death into life. Crossing the Jordan on dry ground, like the Red Sea, is taken up in the New Testament as a picture of baptism and of passing from death to the promised inheritance.
basic.christ: The ark carried the presence of God into the deadly flood so that the people could pass safely; Jesus, God present with us, went down into death itself so that all who follow Him pass safely through. As Joshua was exalted in the sight of Israel, so the Father exalts the greater Joshua, raising Him and setting Him over His people forever.
basic.god: God is the living God, Lord of all the earth, sovereign over the flooding river and over the nations of Canaan. He goes before His people; He requires holiness; and He acts so that all the peoples of the earth may know His mighty hand. The whole crossing is His doing, not Israel's.
basic.crossReferences: Exodus 14 tells of the Red Sea crossing this miracle deliberately echoes. Psalm 114 sings of the sea fleeing and the Jordan turning back before the LORD. 1 Corinthians 10 reads Israel's crossings as pictures for the church. And Hebrews 4 shows the land as a shadow of the rest in Christ.
basic.oneStory: God brings His people across the barrier of the Jordan by going before them in the ark, just as He brought them through the Red Sea. It is another decisive step into the promised inheritance, and it points to Christ, God with us, who leads His people through death into the rest that remains.

context.literary:
Chapter 3 is organized around a single repeated term, the ark of the covenant, named some nine times in seventeen verses, more concentrated than almost any comparable stretch in the Old Testament; the narrator wants the reader's eye fixed on the ark rather than on Joshua, the priests, or the people, since it is the ark's movement that drives every other movement in the scene. The chapter also delays its climax with unusual patience: verses 1 to 13 consist almost entirely of instruction and anticipation, officers passing among the tribes, Joshua explaining what is about to happen, before a single foot touches the river in verse 15. That structure forces the reader to wait exactly as Israel waited, camped for three days, verse 2, before the word became event.

The scene consciously echoes Exodus 14 while reversing its sequence. At the Red Sea the waters divide before Israel advances, a wall on the right and the left already standing when the people step onto the seabed, Exodus 14:22. Here the instruction is explicit that the priests' feet must touch the water's edge before it heaps up, verse 13, so the miracle is reported only after, not before, the step of faith. The narrator has taken a scene his readers already know by heart and reordered its parts to make obedience precede sight, a change too deliberate to be accidental.
context.historical:
The Jordan's spring flood was not a minor inconvenience but a serious natural barrier: fed by snowmelt from Mount Hermon far to the north and swollen by seasonal rain, the river routinely overran its banks in the weeks around barley harvest, precisely the season this crossing occurs in, so that fording it safely, let alone marching a whole nation and its livestock across, was not something any army of the period would have attempted by choice. Ancient Near Eastern armies generally timed campaigns for after harvest or during low water, when river crossings and supply lines were manageable; Israel enters at the worst possible hydrological moment, which is exactly the point.

The two thousand cubit gap the officers set between the people and the ark, roughly a thousand yards, verse 4, was wide enough that the whole camp, spread along the riverbank in tribal order, could keep the ark in view without crowding the priests who carried Israel's most sacred object; a gap of ordinary reverence became, that day, the width every eye needed to watch the miracle unfold. The priests who carried the ark were Levites of the priestly line permitted to bear it on their shoulders using its carrying poles, a task hedged with strict rules elsewhere, since even the ordinary Kohathite Levites who transported the ark on the march were forbidden to touch it directly on pain of death, Numbers 4:15, which sharpens the wonder that these priests were commanded to walk it directly into the river and stand there for hours while a whole nation passed.
context.canonical:
The Jordan becomes something of a theological doorway across the rest of the Old Testament, each later crossing recalling this one. Elijah and Elisha part the same river with a rolled up cloak, the company of prophets watching from a distance just as Israel once watched the ark, and the question the sons of the prophets ask afterward, where is the LORD, the God of Elijah, 2 Kings 2:8 and 2:14, is really the same question this chapter is designed to answer for Israel: is the LORD who acted for Moses also acting now? Naaman the Syrian commander is told to wash seven times in this same river to be cleansed of leprosy, 2 Kings 5:10 to 14, so that the Jordan becomes, in miniature, a place where obedience to God's specific word, however strange it looks, brings a deliverance no human effort could produce, the same lesson the priests' feet in the flood already taught.

Centuries later John the Baptist preaches and baptizes at the Jordan, and Jesus comes to that river to be baptized, Matthew 3:13 to 17, entering the water at the very boundary His people once crossed into their inheritance, before He is driven into the wilderness to succeed where Israel failed. The New Testament writers who read Israel's story as a pattern for the church, most explicitly Paul in 1 Corinthians 10, treat crossings like this one as real events with a real afterlife in Christian instruction, warning believers not to presume on privilege while pointing them to a greater deliverance already accomplished in Jesus.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The author places this miracle right where Israel's confidence would be most fragile, on the far bank of an obstacle their fathers never had to face, under a leader who has never yet led them into danger. Verse 7's promise, that God will begin to exalt Joshua so all Israel may know the LORD is with him as He was with Moses, reveals a pastoral purpose behind the miracle as much as a theological one: the author wants readers to see that God supplies public, undeniable confirmation precisely at the point where a nation's trust in its leadership could otherwise crack.

The instruction that the people keep a careful distance from the ark, verse 4, because they have never traveled this way before, teaches by its very wording that this generation is not simply repeating their fathers' exodus; they are being led into genuinely new territory, and the author wants them, and every later reader, to learn that unfamiliar ground is exactly where the presence of God, not previous experience, must lead. The whole account is written so that obedience to unfamiliar instructions, following the ark rather than one's own sense of the way, becomes the mark of a people who trust the God who goes before them.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The particular details, a two thousand cubit gap, priests specifically from the tribe of Levi, three full days of preparation, describe how this one crossing was carried out and are not fresh commands binding on believers today; no later chapter of Scripture repeats the exact measurements as a rule for approaching holy things. What is rightly drawn from the account is the shape of genuine faith it displays: the priests act on a specific word God had actually spoken to Joshua, not on a general hope that water might part if enough faith is exercised.

That distinction matters for how the passage is used. It is not a template for expecting a miracle whenever a believer steps toward danger; it is a lesson that God's people move forward on God's revealed word, however unfamiliar the ground, and let the outcome belong to Him rather than demanding to see the outcome first.

debates.question: Why did God have the ark go first into the river rather than simply parting the water as at the Red Sea?

views.label: To center the whole event on God's presence
views.case: By sending the ark, the throne of God's presence, ahead into the flood, God makes unmistakably clear that it is His presence, not Joshua's staff or Israel's strength, that opens the way; the people follow God into the land, and the priests stand in the riverbed holding the ark until all have passed, a vivid picture of the LORD Himself bearing His people across.

views.label: To require a step of faith before the miracle
views.case: Unlike the Red Sea, where the water parted before Israel moved, here the priests must step into the flooding river first, and only then does the water heap up; the sequence teaches that God's people advance by faith, acting on His word before they see the deliverance.

debates.bearing: Both readings converge: the crossing magnifies God's leading presence and calls His people to follow that presence in faith, trusting the promise before the waters part.

debates.question: Did God work through a natural mechanism at the Jordan, and if so, does that make the crossing less miraculous?

views.label: God used the land itself as His instrument
views.case: The unstable clay banks upstream near Adam and Zarethan have been known in later history to collapse and dam the river's flow for a period after earthquakes, and some readers see God timing and directing exactly such a collapse at the moment the priests' feet touched the water, so that the physical means was real while the timing, the word given in advance, and the miles of dry riverbed downstream where the priests stood were entirely supernatural.

views.label: The miracle needs no natural explanation
views.case: Others resist looking for a mechanism at all, noting that the text gives no hint of an upstream cause and reads as a direct act of God on the water itself, cut off and standing up in a heap, verse 13, a description that asks to be read as a sheer act of divine power rather than an assisted natural event.

debates.bearing: Either way the chapter's own explanation is theological rather than geological: whatever secondary means God may have used, the text credits the crossing entirely to the LORD acting through the ark, so that Israel's confidence rests on His spoken word and not on an explanation of how the water actually stopped.

study.originalLanguages:
Beyond qadash, aron, and chay, several other words shape the chapter's message. Twice the ark is called the ark of the Lord of all the earth, adon kol ha'arets, verses 11 and 13, a title bigger than covenant Lord of Israel alone; the same title appears again in only a handful of places, among them Micah 4:13, where the LORD of all the earth judges the nations, and it fits this scene exactly, since the miracle is staged so that a title normally reserved for Israel's God among Israel becomes, in the mouths of Joshua and the narrator, a claim over the whole earth's waters and the whole earth's future inhabitants of Canaan.

Joshua tells the people that tomorrow the LORD will do niphla'oth, wonders, among them, verse 5, the standard Hebrew word for acts that exceed ordinary explanation, the same word used of the plagues on Egypt, Exodus 3:20, and celebrated throughout the Psalms as the mark of God's own unmistakable action, Psalm 78:4 already calling them by this name. Calling the coming event a wonder before it happens sets the reader's expectation precisely: this will not be a natural crossing helped along by God, it will be the kind of act Israel already associates with the exodus itself.

When the water finally stops, verses 13 and 16 say it will stand up, or already stands up, in a ned, a heap. The same rare word describes the Red Sea in the victory song of Exodus 15:8, the floods stood upright like a heap, and it surfaces again in Psalm 78:13, remembering that same crossing. The author of Joshua reaches for the identical term used for the first great water miracle to describe the second, so that the vocabulary itself, not only the narrative shape, binds the Jordan to the Red Sea as one continuous act of the same God.

The waters are also described as cut off, from the common verb karath, the same root that stands behind the Hebrew idiom to cut a covenant, karath berith, used throughout the Pentateuch for making a binding agreement. Whether or not the author intends a deliberate pun, the coincidence is suggestive: the very verb that describes covenants being solemnly established is used here for a river being solemnly, decisively stopped, so that even the grammar of the miracle carries the flavor of covenant, a sign sealed rather than a mere pause in nature.

One more verb rewards attention. The priests are said to stand firm, from amad, on dry ground in the middle of the riverbed, verse 17, the same ordinary verb used throughout the Old Testament for standing one's ground, standing before the LORD, or a servant standing ready to obey. Its very ordinariness is the point: while the extraordinary word for wonder describes what God does to the water, the plain, everyday verb amad describes what the priests do, they simply stand where they are told, for as long as they are told, while a whole nation crosses. The miracle belongs to God's word and God's power; the priests' part is the plainest kind of obedience, holding a position rather than performing an act.

typology.type: The ark, God's presence, going first into the deadly flood
typology.fulfillment: The priests do not merely accompany the ark; they carry it into the flood first and remain standing there, bearing it, until the last Israelite has passed, verse 17. Christ's own descent into death works the same way: He goes first into the deep water none of His people could survive alone, and He remains there, bearing its full weight, until the way through is entirely open, Hebrews 2:14 to 15. John's Gospel makes the connection explicit when Jesus tells Martha, I am the resurrection and the life, whoever believes in Me will live, even though he dies, John 11:25. The type is not exact: the ark was carried by priests who themselves needed shelter from the flood, while Christ needed no one to carry Him through death and emerged from it under His own authority, John 10:18.

typology.type: Israel crossing the waters into the inheritance
typology.fulfillment: Paul tells the Corinthians that Israel's fathers were all baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea, and reads their whole wilderness journey as written down for our instruction, 1 Corinthians 10:1 to 2 and 10:11; the Jordan crossing belongs to the same pattern one step further along, a passage through water that marks entry into what God had promised rather than merely escape from what enslaved. The New Testament takes up the picture of passing through water into a new standing in baptism itself, buried and raised with Christ, Romans 6:3 to 4. The type falls short of a strict equation, since baptism does not itself accomplish what Christ's death and resurrection accomplish, it signifies and seals a passage that has already happened in union with Him, rather than parting any literal water.

typology.type: God exalting Joshua before all Israel
typology.fulfillment: The LORD's promise, today I will begin to exalt you in the sight of all Israel, verse 7, is fulfilled publicly and unmistakably the moment the water stops, so that Joshua's authority rests entirely on an act only God could perform, not on Joshua's own claim to succeed Moses. Paul describes the far greater exaltation of Jesus in almost identical terms of public vindication: God highly exalted Him and gave Him the name above every name, so that every knee will bow and every tongue confess Him Lord, Philippians 2:9 to 11. Joshua's exaltation lasts one generation and secures one conquest; the type is finally too small, since the exaltation of Christ is once for all, over every power, and unto the glory of God the Father forever, with no successor required after Him.

typology.type: Israel following a path they had never traveled before, guided only by the ark ahead of them, Joshua 3:4
typology.fulfillment: The officers' instruction is remarkably candid: keep your distance and watch the ark, since you have never been this way before. Israel does not know the road; they know only the presence that leads it. The writer of Hebrews describes exactly this kind of faith as the substance of things hoped for, the conviction of things not seen, Hebrews 11:1, and Paul says believers walk by faith, not by sight, 2 Corinthians 5:7. The type is imperfect because Israel could still see the ark itself with their own eyes, a visible guide for an unseen road, while the church walks by trust in a Christ who is not physically visible at all, present instead by His Spirit and His word.

study.christ:
Joshua and Jesus share a name before they share a mission; Iesous, the Greek form of Yehoshua, is the very word the Septuagint uses for Joshua throughout this book, so that the writer of Hebrews can build an entire argument on the fact that Joshua could not be the last word: if Joshua had given them rest, God would not have spoken later about another day, Hebrews 4:8. This chapter is exactly the moment Joshua's rest begins, a hard won crossing into an inheritance still full of enemies to be fought; it points forward to a greater Joshua whose rest, once entered, needs no further conquest, Hebrews 4:9 to 10.

The chapter's center of gravity is not Joshua at all but the ark going ahead into water no ordinary traveler could cross safely at flood stage. That is itself a small picture of the larger pattern of the incarnation: God does not send Israel into danger and wait to see if they manage; He goes first, in visible, carried form, into the very danger His people must pass through. The eternal Son does this completely and finally, taking on flesh and blood so that through death He might destroy the one who holds the power of death, and free those who through fear of death were subject to slavery their whole lives, Hebrews 2:14 to 15. What the ark pictured in wood and gold overlaid, carried by priests who trembled to touch it, Christ accomplished in His own body, entering death itself and not merely standing beside it until others passed.

The living God of verse 10, contrasted so sharply with Canaan's lifeless idols, is the same God who raises the dead. Jesus stands at Lazarus' tomb and calls Himself, not merely a worker of resurrections, but the resurrection and the life itself, so that whoever believes in Him will live even though he dies, John 11:25 to 26, a claim no idol of wood or stone could make and no army could confirm the way Israel's crossing confirmed the living God among them. Every element of this chapter, the presence that leads, the exaltation that follows obedience, the rest that still lies ahead, converges on Him: the true and greater Joshua who does not merely lead His people to the edge of an inheritance but secures it for them completely and walks them the entire way through.
study.god:
The seven nations named in verse 10, Canaanites, Hittites, Hivites, Perizzites, Girgashites, Amorites, and Jebusites, are not a random inventory; the same list, in nearly the same order, is the list God gave to Abraham as the peoples whose land his descendants would inherit, Genesis 15:19 to 21. Reciting it here, at the very moment the ark steps into the flood, God is showing Israel that this crossing is the fulfillment, name for name, of a promise sworn some four centuries earlier to a man who owned not one square foot of the land himself. The number seven, the customary sign of fullness in Hebrew thought, underlines the point: this is the whole land, promised whole, being given whole, to a whole nation, exactly as spoken.

This God is also willing to risk His own reputation on a single event. Verse 10 stakes everything on the crossing: this is how you will know that the living God is among you and that He will surely drive out the nations before you. If the river does not stop, the claim is falsified in front of the entire camp and every watching enemy; God ties His own credibility to a specific, publicly verifiable act rather than to a private assurance only Joshua could vouch for. That is a God confident enough in His own power to stake His name on something the whole nation can watch fail or succeed with their own eyes.

And He is a God who works for an audience wider than Israel. The purpose given later in this same story, that all the peoples of the earth may know that the hand of the LORD is mighty, Joshua 4:24, is already implicit in the public, undeniable nature of this crossing: news of a river stopping in full flood, in daylight, before a nation of witnesses, was never going to stay a private testimony. God's actions in this chapter are aimed past Israel to Canaan, and past Canaan to every later reader who has ever asked whether His promises can be trusted to the letter, this many centuries later, exactly as they were first spoken.

crossReferences.note: Moses stretches out his hand and the sea divides into a wall on the right and the left before Israel steps onto the seabed; Joshua's crossing deliberately reverses the order, since here the priests step into the flood first and the water stops only afterward.

The psalm asks the sea and the Jordan directly why they fled and turned back, treating both water crossings as one continuous testimony to the presence of the LORD rather than two unrelated events separated by forty years.

God had already promised Joshua no one would stand against him and that He would never leave him, just as with Moses; the Jordan crossing is the public, undeniable proof that this private promise to Joshua was true.

Paul reads Israel's passage through the sea under the cloud as a baptism into Moses, treating the wilderness generation's water crossings as patterns written for the instruction of the New Testament church.

The writer argues that Joshua's conquest could not be the final rest God promised, since Scripture later speaks of another day of rest still to come, a rest that remains for the people of God in Christ.

God's covenant promise to Abram lists these same seven peoples by name centuries before the crossing; Joshua 3:10 recites the list again as the crossing begins, showing the invasion fulfills an old, specific promise.

Kohathite Levites who normally carried the ark on the march were forbidden even to touch it directly, on pain of death; the priests who carry it into the Jordan and stand there for hours perform an extraordinary, commanded exception.

Elisha later strikes the same river with Elijah's cloak and it parts, asking where is the LORD, the God of Elijah; the Jordan miracle becomes a recurring proof that the God of the exodus and the conquest still acts.

Jesus comes to be baptized at the very river Israel once crossed into the land, and the Father's voice names Him beloved Son, before He is driven into the wilderness to succeed where the first generation failed.

study.oneStory:
From the pillar of cloud and fire that led Israel out of Egypt, Exodus 13:21, to the ark that leads them into Canaan, the whole wilderness generation only ever moves where God's visible presence goes first; this chapter is the last great installment of a pattern begun at the Red Sea and completed, for this stage of the story, at the Jordan. It answers a question the exodus itself left open: getting a people out of slavery is not the same as getting them into an inheritance, and Joshua 3 shows that the same God who accomplishes the first also accomplishes the second, so that redemption is never left half finished.

The chapter also quietly quiets a fear every hearer of Israel's story would carry: the fear that God's presence, once withdrawn at Sinai's boundary or hedged behind priestly restriction, might never again be safe to approach. Here that same presence walks directly into a flood and stands there for the length of an entire nation's crossing, near enough to touch, and no one dies for it; holiness that once demanded distance now leads from the front. Hebrews later calls Jesus a forerunner who has entered before us on our behalf, Hebrews 6:19 to 20, using almost exactly the shape of this scene, someone who goes first into a place we could not survive so that the way is secure when we follow.

The story does not end with a river crossed. It ends, in Revelation's vision of the new creation, with a river of the water of life flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb, with nothing further to cross and no more sea to separate, Revelation 22:1 to 2 and Revelation 21:1. The Jordan that had to be stopped for a night, so that God's people could pass through it once, gives way to a river that will simply flow forever, because the barrier between God and His people has been removed for good, not merely paused for a crossing.

quiz.q: What went ahead of the people into the Jordan?

options.text: The ark of the covenant, carried by the priests, the sign of God's presence.
options.note: Verses 6 and 11 to 17 make the ark leading the way the center of the crossing.

options.text: Joshua alone, holding up his staff over the water.
options.note: Moses raised a staff at the Red Sea; here it is the ark of God's presence that leads, not Joshua's staff.

options.text: The armed men of the eastern tribes as a vanguard.
options.note: The eastern tribes did cross armed, but what led the way into the river was the ark.

options.text: A pillar of fire moving over the river.
options.note: The pillar guided in the wilderness; here God's presence leads through the ark.

quiz.q: When did the waters of the Jordan pile up?

options.text: As soon as the priests carrying the ark stepped into the water's edge.
options.note: Verses 15 to 16 show the water stopped only after the priests stepped in, a step of faith.

options.text: The night before, so the riverbed was dry by morning.
options.note: The crossing happened as they advanced, not the night before; the water parted when the priests stepped in.

options.text: After the whole nation had already begun wading across.
options.note: The water heaped up first, when the priests' feet touched it, so the people could cross on dry ground.

options.text: Only after Joshua struck the river with a rod.
options.note: No rod is struck; the water stood still when the priests bearing the ark stepped in.

quiz.q: What did the miracle prove, according to Joshua?

options.text: That the living God was among them and would drive out the nations before them.
options.note: Verse 10 states the crossing would show the living God was present and powerful to give the land.

options.text: That Joshua was a greater leader than Moses had been.
options.note: It showed God was with Joshua as with Moses, confirming him, not that he surpassed Moses.

options.text: That Israel's engineers had mastered the river.
options.note: It was a divine miracle, not human skill; the point was the living God among them.

options.text: That the Canaanite gods were also powerful.
options.note: The opposite: the living God is contrasted with the lifeless idols of the nations.

quiz.q: Why did God call the people to consecrate themselves first?

options.text: Because they were about to meet the holy God who would do wonders among them.
options.note: Verse 5 ties consecration to encountering God's mighty, holy presence, as at Sinai.

options.text: Because they needed to rest before the hard crossing.
options.note: Consecration is about holiness before God, not physical rest before exertion.

options.text: Because they had to purify the river before entering it.
options.note: They consecrated themselves, not the river; the point was readiness to meet the holy God.

options.text: Because consecration had nothing to do with the crossing.
options.note: It was directly tied to it: consecrate yourselves, for tomorrow the LORD will do wonders.

quiz.q: How does the crossing point to Christ?

options.text: God's presence went first into the deadly flood so His people could pass, as Christ went into death so His people pass to life.
options.note: The ark bearing God's presence into the waters foreshadows Christ, God with us, John 11:25.

options.text: It shows that God only helps those strong enough to cross on their own.
options.note: The crossing was wholly God's doing; the point is God leading, not human strength.

options.text: It teaches that the land itself is the final goal of salvation.
options.note: The land is a shadow of the greater rest in Christ, not the final goal.

options.text: It has no bearing on Christ or the gospel.
options.note: The ark leading through the waters clearly foreshadows Christ leading His people through death to life.

questions: The priests had to step into the flooding river before the waters parted. Where is God calling you to act on His promise before you can see how it will work out?
Israel followed the ark, God's presence, into a way they had never traveled before. How does it steady you to know that God goes ahead of you into the unknown?
Joshua called the people to consecrate themselves before God acted. What might it look like to prepare your heart to meet God rather than approaching Him casually?
God worked the miracle so that all the peoples of the earth would know His mighty hand. How does remembering that God's purposes are for His glory reshape the way you pray about your own needs?

The ark carried God's presence into the deadly waters ahead of the people, foreshadowing Christ going into death for us. How does Jesus going before you into the hardest places give you courage this week?

translationNotes.note: Two thousand cubits is about 3,000 feet or 914 meters, as the BSB footnote notes; the gap kept the holy ark visible yet set apart from the people.
The Sea of the Arabah, the Salt Sea, is the Dead Sea, as the BSB footnote notes; the water backed up far upstream near the city of Adam.
